questions.stem: When the government uses taxes and transfer payments to reduce gaps between rich and poor, it is performing its role of:
options: regulation
redistribution
stabilisation
reallocation
questions.explanation: Redistribution changes the distribution of income, for example through progressive taxes and pensions. Stabilisation smooths the business cycle, and reallocation shifts resources between uses.

questions.stem: The government taxes tobacco heavily and subsidises public transport, shifting resources away from one use and towards another. This is its role of:
options: reallocation
redistribution
stabilisation
privatisation
questions.explanation: Reallocation changes what is produced by altering incentives or providing goods directly. Redistribution concerns who receives income, not which goods are produced.

questions.stem: During a recession, the government increases spending to support jobs and incomes. This reflects its role of:
options: redistribution
nationalisation
stabilisation
reallocation
questions.explanation: Stabilisation aims to reduce fluctuations in the business cycle, keeping unemployment and inflation low. Spending more in downturns and less in booms smooths activity.

questions.stem: Economists describe governments as social welfare-maximising agents. This means governments aim to:
options: improve the community's overall quality of life, not just raise output
maximise their own revenue by setting the highest tax rates the economy can bear
maximise the profits of government-owned businesses before providing any services
maximise the welfare payments made to each household regardless of need
questions.explanation: Governments weigh the wellbeing of the whole community, including equity, health and the environment, in making decisions. Unlike firms, their goal is not profit.

questions.stem: Which is the best example of regulation as a government tool to minimise harm?
options: A cash payment to families with young children
A tax on the sale of new passenger cars
A government-owned company building roads
Mandatory safety standards for child car seats
questions.explanation: Regulations are rules that require or prohibit actions, here to reduce the risk of injury. Cash payments are transfers, a tax changes prices, and a government company is direct provision.

questions.stem: The government sends households a letter showing that most of their neighbours pay their tax on time. This is an example of:
options: a nudge
a regulation
a tax incentive
a transfer payment
questions.explanation: Nudges use insights from behavioural economics, here social norms, to change behaviour without changing rules or financial incentives. A tax incentive changes the financial reward for an action.

questions.stem: Which is an example of an incentive used by government to change behaviour?
options: A rebate for households installing home batteries
A ban on smoking in all indoor workplaces
A reminder text message to vote on election day
A legal requirement to wear a seatbelt in cars
questions.explanation: An incentive changes the financial payoff, here lowering the cost of a battery. A ban and a legal requirement are regulations, and a reminder message is a nudge.

questions.stem: Which is an argument for the privatisation of a government-owned business?
options: The business earns a steady flow of revenue for the government
Essential services should not be run for private profit
Private owners facing competition may operate it more efficiently
Government ownership ensures services reach unprofitable regions
questions.explanation: Supporters argue that the profit motive and competition improve efficiency and service, and the sale raises funds. The other options are arguments for keeping, or nationalising, a business.

questions.stem: A government considers nationalising a privately owned electricity network that is a natural monopoly. The strongest argument for doing so is that:
options: it could prevent the owner from using its market power to charge high prices
it would introduce competition by allowing new firms to build rival networks
it would raise more revenue because private firms are taxed at lower rates
it would remove the need for any regulation of electricity prices
questions.explanation: With only one network, a private owner can exploit monopoly power; public ownership lets the government set prices in the community's interest. Critics argue that regulation of a private owner can achieve the same at lower cost.

questions.stem: Which Australian businesses were fully privatised by the federal government?
options: NBN Co and the Reserve Bank
Medicare and the Tax Office
Qantas and the Commonwealth Bank
Australia Post and the ABC
questions.explanation: Qantas and the Commonwealth Bank were sold in the 1990s, and Telstra was privatised in stages from 1997. Australia Post, the ABC and NBN Co remain government-owned.

questions.stem: The federal Budget is:
options: the government's plan of revenue and spending for the coming financial year
the Reserve Bank's annual decision on the cash rate for the coming financial year
a record of all goods and services traded between Australia and other countries
the total amount of debt owed by Australian households to the banking system
questions.explanation: The Treasurer usually delivers the Budget in May, setting out estimates of receipts and outlays for the financial year from 1 July and for the following years. The cash rate is set by the RBA.

questions.stem: The tax-transfer system redistributes income mainly by:
options: taxing lower incomes at higher rates to fund services for all households
taxing higher incomes at higher rates and paying benefits to those in need
taxing all incomes at the same rate and paying benefits to everyone equally
taxing only businesses and paying their profits to low-income households
questions.explanation: A progressive income tax collects proportionally more from higher earners, while targeted payments such as the age pension and JobSeeker go to those with low incomes. Together they narrow income gaps.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a transfer payment?
options: Payment to a construction firm for a new road
The purchase of new equipment for the army
The age pension paid to an eligible retiree
A salary paid to a public school teacher
questions.explanation: Transfer payments move income to people without any good or service being provided in return. Salaries and purchases of goods are payments for services or output.

questions.stem: Which is the largest single source of revenue for the Australian Government?
options: Company income tax
Excise on fuel
Customs duty on imports
Individual income tax
questions.explanation: Taxes on individuals' incomes raise far more than any other source, with company tax the next largest. This heavy reliance on income tax is one argument made for tax reform.

questions.stem: Which tax is levied on consumption?
options: Capital gains tax
The goods and services tax (GST)
Personal income tax
Company income tax
questions.explanation: The GST is a 10% tax on most goods and services, collected at each stage of sale and passed to the states. Income, company and capital gains taxes are levied on income.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the tax base?
options: It is the lowest rate of tax that any taxpayer must pay each year
It is the group of taxpayers who pay no tax at all in a given year
It is the total tax revenue collected by government in a year
It is what a tax is levied on, such as income, wealth or consumption
questions.explanation: Taxes can be levied on income (such as income tax), wealth (such as land tax) or consumption (such as GST and excise). A broad base lets a given revenue be raised with lower rates.

questions.stem: A tax paid directly to the government by the person on whom it is levied, such as income tax, is:
options: an excise duty
a direct tax
an indirect tax
a regressive tax
questions.explanation: Direct taxes are levied on income or wealth and cannot easily be passed on. Indirect taxes, such as GST and excise, are collected from businesses and largely passed on in prices.

questions.stem: Excise duty is best described as:
options: a tax on the total value of wealth held by households
a tax on all goods and services at a uniform rate
a tax on specific goods such as fuel, alcohol and tobacco
a tax on the profits earned by Australian companies
questions.explanation: Excise is charged per unit on selected goods, often to raise revenue and discourage harmful consumption. A uniform tax on most goods and services is the GST.

questions.stem: A tobacco company is legally required to pay excise to the government, but it raises its prices so that smokers bear most of the cost. This shows that:
options: the economic incidence falls on the company but the legal incidence falls mainly on consumers
both the legal and the economic incidence fall entirely on the company
both the legal and the economic incidence fall entirely on consumers
the legal incidence falls on the company but the economic incidence falls mainly on consumers
questions.explanation: Legal incidence is who must pay the tax to the government; economic incidence is who actually bears it. Because demand for tobacco is inelastic, firms can pass most of the tax on to buyers.

questions.stem: A tax is regressive when:
options: it takes a larger share of income from high-income earners than low-income earners
it takes the same share of income from earners at every level of income
it is collected only from people with incomes above a set threshold
it takes a larger share of income from low-income earners than high-income earners
questions.explanation: Consumption taxes such as the GST are regressive because low-income households spend a larger share of their income. A tax taking a larger share from high earners is progressive.

questions.stem: Personal income tax in Australia is progressive. This means that:
options: people on low incomes pay a higher average rate
the tax rate falls as taxable income rises
the average tax rate rises as taxable income rises
every taxpayer pays the same percentage of income
questions.explanation: Higher slices of income are taxed at higher marginal rates, so the average rate increases with income. Equal rates for everyone would be a proportional, or flat, tax.

questions.stem: Taxpayer A earns $50,000 and pays $7,500 tax; Taxpayer B earns $150,000 and pays $37,500. Their average tax rates are:
options: 15% and 25%, so the tax is progressive
15% and 25%, so the tax is regressive
25% and 15%, so the tax is progressive
15% and 15%, so the tax is proportional
questions.explanation: Average tax rate = tax / income: 7,500 / 50,000 = 15% and 37,500 / 150,000 = 25%. Because the higher earner pays a larger share of income, the tax is progressive.

questions.stem: Which is a feature of a good tax?
options: Complexity: it has many exemptions for particular groups
Inefficiency: it changes behaviour as much as possible
Uncertainty: its amount changes without warning each year
Simplicity: it is easy to understand, pay and collect
questions.explanation: A good tax is simple, fair and efficient. Many exemptions add complexity and opportunities for avoidance, and a good tax distorts economic decisions as little as possible.

questions.stem: A tax is described as efficient if it:
options: changes consumer behaviour as much as possible in every market it covers
raises revenue while distorting economic decisions as little as possible
raises the largest possible revenue regardless of the effect on behaviour
is collected from as few taxpayers as possible to save on administration
questions.explanation: Efficient taxes cause little change to work, saving and investment decisions, so they cost the economy little beyond the revenue raised. Broad-based taxes on immobile bases, such as land, tend to be efficient.

questions.stem: Horizontal equity in taxation means that:
options: taxes should be set so that every income group receives equal benefits
people with the same capacity to pay should pay the same amount of tax
people with greater capacity to pay should pay more tax than others
every person should pay exactly the same dollar amount of tax
questions.explanation: Horizontal equity treats people in similar situations alike. Vertical equity, that those able to pay more should pay more, underlies progressive taxation.

questions.stem: Which is a rationale often given for reforming Australia's tax system?
options: The fact that all income is taxed at one flat rate, which is regarded as unfair
Heavy reliance on income tax, while an ageing population shrinks the share of workers
Very low reliance on income tax, while a younger population raises the share of workers
The absence of any tax on consumption, which leaves government with too little revenue
questions.explanation: As the population ages, fewer workers support more retirees, so revenue tied to wages comes under pressure. Bracket creep and falling fuel excise as vehicles electrify are other reasons given for reform.

questions.stem: As incomes rise with inflation, more of each taxpayer's income falls into higher tax brackets, even though real income has not risen. This is called:
options: crowding out
bracket creep
the paradox of thrift
the free rider problem
questions.explanation: Bracket creep raises the average tax rate without any change in tax law, increasing the tax burden over time. Governments periodically adjust thresholds or cut rates to return it.

questions.stem: Which is a main purpose of taxation?
options: Ensuring that every household has exactly the same disposable income
Fixing the prices of goods and services sold by private businesses
Reducing the money supply so that interest rates rise each year
Raising revenue to fund government services and transfer payments
questions.explanation: Taxes fund spending on services such as health and education, and also redistribute income and change behaviour. Interest rates are set through monetary policy, not taxation.

questions.stem: Spending on the wages of public servants and the day-to-day running of hospitals is:
options: a transfer payment
recurrent spending
non-recurrent spending
capital spending
questions.explanation: Recurrent spending covers ongoing costs that occur every year. Non-recurrent, or capital, spending is on long-lived assets such as new roads, schools and hospitals.

questions.stem: Which is an example of non-recurrent government spending?
options: Making age pension payments to retirees
Buying medical supplies for public hospitals
Building a new rail line between two cities
Paying the salaries of police officers each fortnight
questions.explanation: A new rail line is a one-off capital investment that provides services over many years. Salaries, pensions and supplies are recurrent costs.

questions.stem: Which is the largest area of Australian Government spending?
options: Transport and communication
Social security and welfare
Defence
Education
questions.explanation: Social security and welfare, including the age pension, family payments and the NDIS, is the largest category, followed by health. Defence and education are smaller.

questions.stem: Why do governments spend on infrastructure such as ports and roads?
options: They reduce government debt immediately in the year they are built
They raise productivity and are often under-provided by markets
They are transfer payments that redistribute income to low earners
They are recurrent costs that must be paid every year to employees
questions.explanation: Infrastructure lowers transport and business costs and has public good features, so markets may under-supply it. It is usually financed over many years and can add to debt in the short term.

questions.stem: Which is a rationale for reforming Australian Government spending?
options: Government spending has no effect on economic growth or living standards
All government spending is non-recurrent and so cannot be reduced
Spending on health, aged care and the NDIS is growing faster than revenue
Spending on welfare is shrinking because the population is getting younger
questions.explanation: An ageing population and fast-growing programs put pressure on the budget, prompting calls to improve the efficiency and targeting of spending. The population is ageing, not getting younger.

questions.stem: Spending on essential services such as public hospitals and schools is justified mainly because these services:
options: are common-pool resources that would be overused
are goods for which demand is perfectly elastic
are merit goods that markets would under-provide
are demerit goods that markets would over-provide
questions.explanation: Health and education benefit the wider community and individuals underestimate their value, so a market alone would provide too little. Government provides or subsidises them to raise consumption.

questions.stem: Which combination shows the government performing both its redistribution and stabilisation roles at once?
options: Banning a harmful pesticide during a boom
Raising unemployment benefits during a recession
Raising tobacco excise during an economic boom
Selling a state-owned bank during a recession
questions.explanation: Higher benefits support low-income households (redistribution) and add to spending when demand is weak (stabilisation). Tobacco excise reallocates resources, and a ban is regulation.

questions.stem: A government replaces part of personal income tax with a higher GST, keeping total revenue the same. The most likely criticism is that the change:
options: makes the tax system less progressive, as low earners spend more of their income
makes the tax system more progressive, as high earners spend more of their income
reduces the tax base, as consumption is a narrower base than personal income
raises the economic incidence on companies, as the GST is a tax on profits
questions.explanation: Shifting from a progressive income tax to a regressive consumption tax increases the share of tax paid by low-income households unless compensation is provided. Supporters argue a broad consumption tax is more efficient.

questions.stem: Fuel excise revenue is expected to fall as more motorists switch to electric vehicles. This is a rationale for tax reform because:
options: the tax base is growing, so fuel excise rates can be cut for all motorists
fuel excise is a direct tax, so it cannot be passed on to motorists
fuel excise is the largest source of revenue for the Australian Government
the tax base is shrinking, so revenue for roads must come from another source
questions.explanation: As petrol and diesel use falls, a tax levied per litre raises less, even though electric vehicles still use the roads. Options discussed include road-user charges based on distance driven.
